newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Aid to Bosnia attracts foreign firms -- experts.
newsitem.headline: Aid to Bosnia attracts foreign firms -- experts.

text.p: Foreign firms remain reluctant to pursue direct investment in Bosnia but a growing number of companies are keen to grab a share of reconstruction projects funded by international aid, analysts said on Thursday.

"Bigger companies, at the moment, are interested in the infrastructure projects and they are bluntly interested in Bosnia because of international financing," said Philip Watkins, of the British consultant firm Resolution Partnership.
Most foreign investors are waiting for signs that the fragile peace in Bosnia has taken hold before venturing into private deals, Watkins told Reuters.
"Some see the opportunity to invest but the political situation and the uncertaintly is something that would hold them back from large financial investments of their own," he said.

The international community committed some $2 billion for reconstruction projects in 1996 and a forthcoming donors' conference is expected to raise some $1.4 billion to help Bosnia recover from a devastating war that ended in 1995.
Money raised at this year's conference will target rebuilding the country's transport, power and telephone networks, World Bank officials said.
Donor governments, in particular Germany, are also stressing the need for programmes which create jobs and housing for refugees and displaced persons.
The first phase of reconstruction attracted suppliers who could quickly deliver tractors, buses, asphalt-crushing machines and other equipment for emergency repairs.

The next phase in reconstruction, which will focus on large-scale instrastructure projects, has lured the interest of engineering and construction firms vying for management and procurement contracts, Watkins and other foreign experts said.
"Most of the big projects that are big enough to excite an international company to get involved are only just beginning," Watkins said.
He cited plans to rebuild water supply, railway and power networks and to repair bridges across Bosnia's northern border on the river Sava.
Projects sponsored by the World Bank and other organisations tend to be awarded to those foreign firms that have forged ties with Bosnian companies, he said.
"There is no way that a large company is going to get involved in here without finding a local partner," he said.

Watkins said his consultant firm, which offers a range of business services to interested foreign investors, has started receiving calls from venture capital companies looking for investments with a quick turnaround.

Rory O'Sullivan, director of the World Bank in Bosnia, said the country's wood processing, furniture, footwear and power transmission industries were attracting attention as possible short-term investments.
"There are some gems to pick up in Bosnia and people are looking at them," O'Sullivan said.

Although international aid could repair infrastructure and bring in engineering firms, O'Sullivan said only the adoption of fundamental privatisation reforms could pave the way for major private investment.
"It's not going to be the World Bank pulling this country back to what it was before and then beyond that. It's going to be private sector investment," O'Sullivan said.

"That's why its very important to have an investor friendly environment," he said. International financial authorities were lobbying political leaders to adopt privatisation laws within four to six weeks, he added.
